title: Baron: two applicative acts — mind’s persuasion and will’s ardent love
source_text: LXXV. Nonnulli vero, ut Robertus Baronius, expresse docent fideles, seu renatos, non uno actu, sed duobus actibus, meritum Christi & Dei misericordiam sibi applicare. Prior actus est certa persuasio, seu judicium mentis Dei testimonio nitens, quo apud nos statuimus Salvatorem nostrum Jesum Christum pro nostris peccatis plenissime satisfecisse, & per consequens non solum aliis, sed nobis quoque remissionem peccatorum, aeternam justitiam & vitam donatam esse, idque gratis ex Dei misericordia, propter unius Christi meritum. Posterior actus applicativus gratiae est ardens amor quo voluntas gratiam Dei complectitur, serio expectans perfectionem istius gratiae sensum in hac vita, & claram Dei visionem in futura. Quae verba sunt Baronii in Philosophia Theologiae ancillante, Exercit. 3. Artic. 19. Ubi docet quoque utrumque hunc actum ad fiduciam requiri, quia nemo dici potest confidere, seu fiduciam habere de bono obtinendo, nisi & firmam habeat persuasionem in intellectu, & desiderium vel amorem istius boni in voluntate. Prior tamen actus, juxta ipsum, est ipsa essentia, seu ratio formalis fiduciae; posterior vero est tantum actus ei annexus & concomitans. Unde est etiam quod applicationem gratiae per priorem actum praecipue fieri docet.
pass_a_gloss: But some, as Robert Baron, expressly teach that the faithful, or regenerate, apply to themselves the merit of Christ and God's mercy not by one act, but by two acts. The prior act is a certain persuasion, or judgment of the mind resting on God's testimony, by which we lay down among ourselves that our Savior Jesus Christ has most fully satisfied for our sins, and consequently that not only to others, but also to us, remission of sins, eternal justice, and life have been given — and that freely from God's mercy, for the merit of Christ alone. The posterior applicative act of grace is an ardent love by which the will embraces God's grace, seriously expecting the perfection of the sense of that grace in this life, and the clear vision of God in the future. Which words are Baron's in Philosophy the Handmaid of Theology, Exercise 3, Article 19. Where he also teaches that both this act is required for trust, because no one can be said to trust, or to have trust concerning a good to be obtained, unless he both has a firm persuasion in the intellect, and a desire or love of that good in the will. Yet the prior act, according to him, is the very essence, or formal reason of trust; but the posterior is only an act annexed and accompanying it. Whence also it is that he teaches that the application of grace is chiefly done through the prior act.
pass_b_english: Baron: the regenerate apply Christ’s merit and God’s mercy by two acts, not one.
First: sure mind-persuasion on God’s testimony — Christ has fully satisfied for our sins; remission, eternal justice, and life are given to us too, freely, for Christ’s merit alone.
Second: ardent love — the will embraces grace, looking for fuller sense now and clear vision hereafter.
Both required for fiducia (firm persuasion + desire); yet the first is fiducia’s formal essence, the second only concomitant — so grace is chiefly applied by the prior act.
